messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
David, a 49-year-old City Council Member, had always been proud of his service to his community, but the shadows of his past loomed large over him. He had served in combat, where he witnessed the horrors of war that would forever alter his perception of safety and trust. In the months following his return, he found himself grappling with intrusive memories—the kind that would ambush him in quiet moments when he least expected it. These memories were often disjointed, leaving him with an incomplete picture of the traumatic events. He would try to recount his experiences, but the words would fail him, slipping through his fingers like sand. Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that he had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who he was. It was as though his mind was protecting him from the full weight of what had transpired, but this selective recollection only added to his frustration and sense of disorientation.

David’s memories were not just vague echoes; they were visceral reminders of terror that gripped him tightly. When he recalled the chaos of battle, the same fear he felt back then surged through him, leaving him short of breath. This terror was not merely a memory; it felt like a current that coursed through his body, reminding him that he was still in danger. Such moments often triggered a profound sense of distrust in his environment. Despite reassurances from his family and friends that he was safe, David found it impossible to believe them. The world beyond his front door felt fraught with peril, and his body reacted instinctively as though he were still in combat. This constant state of threat reaffirmed his negative beliefs about himself, whispering to him that he was no longer the same person, that safety was an illusion he could no longer trust. Feeling this afraid all the time, he had eventually come to accept the conclusion his body kept offering: that he was not the kind of person who got to feel safe. He was on constant alert, hypervigilant to any potential threat, leading him to perceive even the most benign interactions—like a gentle touch from his wife—as alarming and intrusive.

To cope with this pervasive sense of danger, David developed maladaptive strategies. He would drown out his racing thoughts and the cacophony of his memories by turning up the volume on the television or blasting loud music throughout the house. He had learned that if he kept the television on loud enough, the memories couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy, and it was in that silence that the horrors of his past would resurface, threatening to consume him. This sensory distraction provided a temporary reprieve from the relentless cycle of his own mind, yet it also left him feeling disconnected from the reality around him. Each time he used these strategies to cope, he felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that he couldn't manage without them, deepening his sense of inadequacy. His attempts to shield himself from the outside world extended to his relationships as well; he avoided any form of physical contact, fearing that unexpected touch would unleash the floodgates of his trauma. Each time someone brushed against him accidentally, he would react with alarm, his heart racing and his breath quickening, which only reinforced his belief that he could not trust anyone or anything.

David's nights were often restless, filled with sleep problems that kept him tossing and turning. The very act of falling asleep felt like stepping into a minefield, with the memories threatening to erupt at any moment. He was caught in a relentless cycle where his body felt like the enemy, betraying him with its responses to perceived threats. On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome. The more he tried to manage his anxiety, the more he became trapped in a web of negative appraisals. The memories that surfaced during these moments only confirmed his fears, leading him to believe that he was permanently vulnerable and incapable of managing his anxiety. He felt that the world was a dangerous place, and he started to view his own reactions as a sign of weakness. This self-criticism only deepened his struggle, creating a feedback loop that magnified his sense of isolation and despair. As David constantly felt threatened by the world around him, he came to believe that he was permanently vulnerable, leading him to view himself as weak and incapable of managing his anxiety.

Over time, David's maladaptive strategies became a way of life. They provided a temporary fix, but they also clouded his memory, making it harder for him to confront the reality of his experiences. Each strategy he employed bolstered his negative beliefs about himself and the world around him, reinforcing the idea that he was forever marked by his past. It was a paradox: in his attempts to protect himself, he had inadvertently entrenched himself deeper in his trauma, unable to see a way out.

As David sat in his office overlooking the city, he realized that he could no longer manage on his own. The weight of his memories and the constant threat they posed had become unbearable. It was during a particularly vivid flashback that he felt a shattering of his resolve, and he knew he needed help. Seeking therapy was his last hope, a desperate bid to reclaim his life from the shadows of his past. What he feared most was that he would never escape the clutches of his trauma, but he also held onto a flicker of hope that healing was possible, that perhaps he could learn to trust the world again.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship between negative appraisals and the sense of threat.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette lacks a connection between memory and negative appraisals, failing to show how memories influence his self-beliefs.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not convey how the sense of threat leads to negative appraisals about himself.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not illustrate how maladaptive strategies contribute to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
This constant state of threat reaffirmed his negative beliefs about himself, whispering to him that he was no longer the same person, that safety was an illusion he could no longer trust. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The unending fear he felt only solidified his belief that he was permanently vulnerable, reinforcing the notion that he had lost the ability to protect himself in a world that seemed increasingly dangerous.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that he had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who he was. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
With each intrusive memory, David found himself spiraling into a deeper self-reproach, leading him to conclude that the trauma had irrevocably marked him as weak and incapable of managing his life.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
This constant state of threat reaffirmed his negative beliefs about himself, whispering to him that he was no longer the same person, that safety was an illusion he could no longer trust. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Every time he felt that familiar tension coil within him, it fed into the narrative that he was fundamentally flawed, a perspective he struggled to challenge despite knowing it was irrational.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
This sensory distraction provided a temporary reprieve from the relentless cycle of his own mind, yet it also left him feeling disconnected from the reality around him. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
These coping strategies, while offering momentary relief, only deepened his sense of inadequacy, convincing him that he was incapable of facing his fears without reliance on these distractions.
<<<END>>>
